overview: I-Kiribati communities sustain island-specific traditions through meeting houses, kinship, fishing, cultivation and skilled making. The cultural community is broader and older than any modern government phase.

items.text: The maneaba is a meeting place for discussion, ceremonies and shared obligations. Elders, village representatives and religious leaders take part in community decisions.
Traditional maneaba roofs use pandanus thatch and coconut-husk rope. Their high roofs and low eaves help create a sheltered, cool meeting space.
Canoe builders use coconut-fibre lashings to join components. Fishing, travel and racing involve different vessel forms, sustained through repair and sailing knowledge.
A1963 film from Tabiteuea documents pandanus fruit steamed, mashed and sun-dried into tuae packages stored as reserve food. It records a specific community practice.
A1963 film documents swamp-taro cultivation on Tabiteuea, with pandanus leaves and other organic and soil materials added around plants.
Dance gestures often evoke birds in flight or on the ground. Community gatherings and canoe racing continue to sustain cultural knowledge.
Kiribati became independent on 12 July 1979, following British protectorate and colonial administration in the Gilbert Islands. These state phases are separate from I-Kiribati cultural continuity.
